title: AI Health Assistants Explained
body:
An AI health assistant is software that uses programmed rules or learned patterns to help with health-related tasks: answering general health questions, reminding a person to take medicines, helping schedule care, or summarizing health information. These assistants vary widely in quality and in what they are built to do, and the most important distinction is between general information and personal medical advice. A general assistant can explain what a condition usually involves; it cannot diagnose a particular person, and its answers should be checked against a clinician or a trusted health source before acting on them, especially where symptoms are new, worsening, or frightening.

Method. The working method for judging an AI health assistant has four checks. First, what is it built to do, and does it state its limits plainly. Second, what sources does it use, and are they named. Third, does it encourage professional care for serious symptoms, or does it reassure without basis. Fourth, what happens to the health information a user types in: is it stored, shared, or used to train the system. An assistant that hides its limits, its sources, or its data practices fails the check even if its answers sound confident.

If symptoms are severe, sudden, or worsening, seek professional or emergency care promptly rather than consulting an assistant first.

title: Evaluating AI Health Answers
body:
Evaluating an AI health answer means checking it the way a careful reader checks any health claim: looking for what it asserts, what evidence it gives, what it leaves out, and whether it fits the person's actual situation. Useful checks include whether the answer names its sources, whether it distinguishes established facts from uncertain or new findings, whether it mentions when to seek professional care, and whether it asks clarifying questions before giving a confident answer. An answer that is confident, detailed, and wrong is more dangerous than an answer that is cautious and incomplete, because confidence discourages checking.

Method. The working method is a four-question check applied to any AI health answer. First, what exactly is claimed, in one sentence. Second, what evidence or source is given for that claim. Third, what important qualifier or alternative is missing. Fourth, what would a clinician or trusted health source need to know before confirming it for this person. If the answer fails the second or fourth question, treat it as a starting point for a professional conversation, not as a conclusion.

title: Wearable Heart Rate Basics
body:
A wearable heart rate monitor, usually on the wrist, estimates heart rate by shining light into the skin and measuring how the reflected light changes with blood flow. For resting heart rate and for steady exercise, these estimates are often reasonably close to a chest strap or clinical monitor, but they are estimates, not medical measurements, and their accuracy falls during vigorous movement, with poor fit, with tattoos or very dark skin in some devices, and with irregular heart rhythms. A wearable is best used for trends over days and weeks, such as a resting rate that is gradually rising or falling, rather than for single readings treated as exact.

Method. The working method for using wearable heart rate data has four steps. First, wear the device snugly as the maker directs, not loose on the wrist. Second, compare readings with how you feel and with activity, rather than reading any single number alone. Third, look at trends over weeks, not day-to-day jumps. Fourth, bring persistent unusual patterns, such as a resting rate that stays high or a rhythm alert that repeats, to a clinician with the device's data, rather than diagnosing from the device alone.

title: Sleep Tracking Limits
body:
A wearable sleep tracker estimates sleep from movement and heart rate patterns, and sometimes from breathing or blood oxygen estimates, rather than measuring brain activity the way a clinical sleep study does. Trackers are generally better at estimating total sleep time and bedtime patterns than at staging sleep into light, deep, and dream phases, where their stage estimates can be substantially wrong for an individual night. The most useful output is therefore the pattern over weeks: bedtimes, wake times, and total sleep duration, and whether those are regular and sufficient, rather than any single night's stage chart treated as a diagnosis.

Method. The working method for using sleep tracker data has four steps. First, wear the device consistently so nights are comparable. Second, focus on bedtime, wake time, and total sleep over weeks. Third, treat stage charts as rough estimates, not as medical results. Fourth, if sleep problems persist, such as loud snoring with breathing pauses, persistent inability to fall or stay asleep, or daytime sleepiness that affects safety, raise them with a clinician, bringing the tracker's pattern as background, not as a diagnosis.

title: Step Counting and Activity Tracking
body:
Step counting is the simplest wearable measure, and also one of the most robust for everyday use: a wrist or pocket device counts rhythmic movement patterns as steps, and while any single day's count can be off by a margin, the pattern over weeks reliably shows whether a person is more or less active than before. Step goals work best as personal trends rather than as universal targets: a person who walks 4,000 steps daily and moves to 6,000 has made a real change, even though a round-number goal from an app may be higher. Activity tracking adds active minutes, distance estimates, and sometimes floors climbed, each with its own error margin, and each more useful as a trend than as an exact figure.

Method. The working method for using step data has four steps. First, wear the device consistently in the same place. Second, record a baseline week without trying to change anything. Third, set a personal target as a modest increase over baseline, not as an app's default goal. Fourth, review weekly averages rather than daily counts, and adjust the target when life changes, such as illness, injury, or a new job, rather than chasing a number through pain or exhaustion.

It is not medical advice about exercise for any individual, and people with heart, joint, or other conditions should discuss activity targets with their clinician. Step counts do not measure activity quality, strength, balance, or flexibility, which matter alongside walking.

title: Blood Oxygen Wearables
body:
Some wearables estimate blood oxygen saturation from light passed through or reflected from the skin, producing a percentage that looks like a clinical measurement. Consumer estimates are less accurate than clinical pulse oximeters, especially during movement, with poor fit, cold hands, nail polish, or darker skin tones in some devices, and a single wearable reading should not be treated as a medical result. The estimates are most useful, if at all, as a rough trend for a person who understands their device's limits, and they are least useful as a reason to delay care: breathlessness or other worrying symptoms need professional assessment whatever a wearable shows.

Method. The working method for using blood oxygen estimates has four steps. First, follow the maker's fit and stillness instructions exactly, since movement ruins the estimate. Second, take readings at rest, not during or just after exertion. Third, look for repeated unusual patterns rather than reacting to one reading. Fourth, bring persistent unusual patterns to a clinician with notes about fit, movement, and symptoms at the time, rather than presenting a single percentage as a finding.

title: Wearable ECG Features
body:
Some wearables offer an electrocardiogram feature that records a short single-lead heart tracing when the wearer holds still and touches the device as directed, and some can flag possible irregular rhythms during wear. These features can be useful as a way to capture a tracing during symptoms and share it with a clinician, but they are not a full clinical ECG, they cannot rule out heart problems, and they can produce false alerts or miss rhythms that occur when the device is not recording. A tracing flagged as possible atrial fibrillation, or any tracing taken during symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness, or chest pain, deserves prompt professional review rather than self-interpretation.

Method. The working method for using wearable ECG features has four steps. First, learn the maker's recording instructions and practice while well, so a symptomatic recording is done correctly. Second, record during symptoms where safe to do so, noting the time and what was felt. Third, save and share the tracing with a clinician rather than interpreting it alone. Fourth, understand the limits: a normal wearable tracing does not exclude heart disease, and an abnormal flag is a prompt for clinical assessment, not a diagnosis.

title: Fall Detection Wearables
body:
Fall detection in wearables and phones uses motion sensors to recognize the pattern of a hard fall followed by stillness, and then offers or sends an alert to emergency contacts or services if the wearer does not respond. The feature helps most for people who live alone or who might be unable to call for help after a fall, and it works best when emergency contacts are set correctly, the device is worn consistently, and the wearer knows how to cancel a false alert. It does not detect every fall, it can alert falsely during vigorous activity, and it is not a substitute for fall prevention, such as home safety changes, strength and balance activity, and medicine reviews with a clinician.

Method. The working method for using fall detection has four steps. First, turn the feature on where offered and set emergency contacts correctly, testing the contact list without triggering a real alert. Second, wear the device consistently, including at home, where most falls happen. Third, learn how to cancel a false alert quickly. Fourth, review the feature after any fall, whether or not it alerted, and discuss fall prevention with a clinician, because a fall is a signal to review causes, not only to rely on detection next time.

title: Personal Genomic Testing Basics
body:
Personal genomic testing, usually from a saliva sample sent to a testing company, reads parts of a person's DNA and reports information that may include ancestry, traits, and, in some tests, health-related variants. The health reports from consumer tests cover only the variants the test looks for, not a person's whole genome, and a result that says a variant was not found means only that the tested variants were not found, not that no risk exists. Results also carry uncertainty: a variant linked to higher risk does not mean disease will occur, and many conditions involve many variants plus environment and lifestyle, so a single genetic result is rarely the whole story.

Method. The working method for approaching a genomic test has four steps. First, decide what question the test should answer, and check whether the test actually covers it. Second, read the company's privacy and data sharing policies before ordering. Third, when results arrive, read the limits section before the headline results, noting which variants were tested and which were not. Fourth, discuss health-related results with a clinician or genetic counselor before making health decisions, bringing the full report rather than a summary.

title: Ancestry Versus Health DNA Results
body:
Ancestry and health DNA results come from the same sample but answer different questions, and confusing them is a common source of misunderstanding. Ancestry results compare a person's DNA with reference populations to estimate geographic origins and to find relatives who share DNA segments, and those estimates change as reference data grows. Health results report variants that research has linked to traits or disease risk, and those links vary in strength: some variants have strong, well-established effects, while others have small effects that add up only with many other factors. A strong ancestry estimate does not imply a health finding, and a health finding does not change ancestry.

Method. The working method for reading results is to separate the two kinds. First, read ancestry results as estimates with ranges, not as exact percentages of identity. Second, read health results variant by variant, noting the strength of each link and the population it was studied in. Third, check whether relatives' information appears in matching features, and consider their privacy before sharing. Fourth, discuss any health result that suggests action with a clinician or genetic counselor, rather than acting on an ancestry-style confidence in a health result.

title: Pharmacogenomics Basics
body:
Pharmacogenomics is the study of how genetic variation affects responses to medicines: how quickly a person breaks down a drug, how strongly they respond, and how likely certain side effects are. Some medicines have well-established genetic guidance, where a test result can help a clinician choose a dose or an alternative drug, while for most medicines genetic guidance is limited or absent, and ordinary clinical factors such as age, kidney and liver function, and other medicines matter more. A pharmacogenomic result is therefore a piece of prescribing information for a clinician to weigh, not a prescription in itself, and it never justifies changing or stopping a medicine without professional advice.

Method. The working method for approaching pharmacogenomic information has four steps. First, check whether the medicine in question actually has established genetic guidance, rather than assuming every medicine does. Second, obtain the result through a clinical route where possible, so it enters the medical record with proper interpretation. Third, share the result with every prescriber, since a result relevant to one medicine may matter for others. Fourth, never change a dose or stop a medicine based on a consumer report alone; discuss the result with the prescribing clinician first.

title: Genomic Privacy Choices
body:
Genomic privacy choices matter because DNA data is uniquely identifying, long-lasting, and shared with relatives by nature: a person's results can reveal information about parents, siblings, and children who never consented to testing. Before testing, the choices to understand are who holds the raw data, whether it can be deleted, whether it is shared for research or with partners, whether law enforcement can request it, and what happens to the data if the company is sold or closes. After testing, choices remain: downloading and deleting stored data where offered, withdrawing research consent where offered, and thinking carefully before uploading results to public matching sites, which create new holders with their own rules.

Method. The working method is a before-and-after privacy check. Before testing, read the privacy and research policies and note the answers to the five questions above. After results arrive, decide what to download, what to keep stored, and what to delete, and record each decision. Before uploading anywhere else, read that site's policy separately. Tell close relatives in general terms that results can affect them, without sharing the results themselves unless you choose to, because their privacy is involved even though they did not test.

Clinical genetic testing ordered by a clinician follows health care privacy rules more closely than consumer testing, and that difference is worth understanding before choosing a testing route.

title: Sharing Genomic Results with Clinicians
body:
Sharing genomic results with a clinician turns a consumer report into clinical information, but the handover needs care: consumer reports use different variant coverage, different interpretation standards, and different quality controls from clinical tests, so a clinician may need to confirm a consumer finding with a clinical test before acting on it. The useful handover includes the full report, the testing company's name and test version, the list of variants tested, and the specific result that prompts the visit, rather than a single headline or a screenshot of one line. A clinician or genetic counselor can then judge whether the finding matters for this person, whether family members should be offered testing, and whether the result belongs in the medical record.

Method. The working method is a handover packet. First, gather the full report, the test version, and the variants-tested list. Second, write one paragraph stating the question: what result worries you or what decision it might affect. Third, bring the packet to the appointment and ask whether clinical confirmation is needed. Fourth, record the clinician's interpretation and any family testing advice. Fifth, file the packet with the clinician's note, so future clinicians start from the interpreted result rather than from the raw consumer report alone.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for sharing genomic results with clinicians. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record as general information about sharing genomic results. It is not medical advice about any result, and a consumer finding should not change medicines, screening, or surgery plans without clinical confirmation and professional advice. If a result suggests a serious condition, seek professional discussion promptly rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

title: AI Triage Tools
body:
AI triage tools sort health concerns into urgency levels, such as self-care, routine care, urgent care, or emergency care, based on symptoms a user enters and on the tool's programmed rules or learned patterns. These tools are designed for general guidance and for directing people to the right level of care, not for diagnosing an individual, and their accuracy depends on the quality of the symptoms entered, the populations they were tested on, and whether they ask follow-up questions when answers are unclear. A triage result that suggests routine care should not override worsening symptoms, and a triage result that suggests emergency care should be followed promptly even if the person feels better at the moment.

Method. The working method for using a triage tool has four steps. First, enter symptoms carefully and completely, including duration and severity. Second, read the urgency recommendation and the reasons given for it. Third, compare the recommendation with how symptoms are changing: worsening symptoms deserve a higher level of care than a static recommendation suggests. Fourth, if the recommendation conflicts with a clinician's prior advice or with common sense about severe symptoms, seek professional care at the higher level and mention the tool's result as background.

title: Wearable Accuracy Factors
body:
Wearable accuracy depends on a chain of factors, and understanding the chain explains why two devices can disagree and why one device can be right on one day and wrong on the next. The factors include fit and placement, movement during measurement, skin and tattoo effects on optical sensors, temperature, battery and sensor condition, and the algorithm that converts raw signals into the displayed number. Different measures have different weak points: step counts suffer from non-walking arm movements, heart rate suffers from vigorous motion, sleep staging suffers from still wakefulness being mistaken for sleep, and oxygen estimates suffer from cold hands and movement. No single accuracy figure describes a device for all measures and all people.

Method. The working method for judging wearable accuracy has four steps. First, identify the measure and its known weak point for this device. Second, control what can be controlled: fit, stillness, and consistent placement. Third, compare the device against a reference where one exists, such as counting steps manually for a short walk or comparing resting heart rate with a manual pulse. Fourth, use the device for trends over weeks rather than for single readings, since trends average out many small errors while single readings do not.

Use and limits. Use this record as general information about wearable accuracy. It is not medical advice, and accuracy for a consumer device is not the same as clinical accuracy: a device can be useful for fitness trends while being unsuitable for medical decisions. title: Choosing a Wearable by Need
body:
Choosing a wearable by need starts from the question the wearer wants answered, not from the device with the longest feature list. A person who wants activity motivation needs comfortable all-day wear and a clear step and activity display. A person who wants sleep patterns needs consistent overnight wear and a readable sleep trend. A person who wants to share heart data with a clinician needs exportable data and a feature the clinician can interpret. A person who wants fall detection needs reliable wearing and correctly set emergency contacts. Battery life, comfort, water resistance, and data export matter more in daily use than a long list of rarely used sensors, and a device that is not worn gives no data at all.

Method. The working method is a needs-first choice. First, write the one question the wearable should answer. Second, list the features that answer that question and ignore the rest. Third, check comfort, battery life, water resistance, and data export for the shortlisted devices. Fourth, check the data practices: what is stored, shared, and deletable. Fifth, try the device for a return-period trial and judge it by whether the question is actually answered in daily life, not by whether its specifications impress.
